```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>",
                      warning = FALSE, message = FALSE,
                      dpi = 150, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4)
library(Rootopia)
library(terra)
```

## Summary

Rootopia turns segmented root images into root traits with a depth axis. It
reads flatbed scans of washed roots and minirhizotron image sequences, cleans
and thins the segmentation, and measures length, diameter, surface, branching
architecture, network topology, turnover between sessions, and soil color and
texture. For a minirhizotron tube it converts pixel position into soil depth
from the tube's diameter, insertion angle and scan resolution, so every trait
can be reported per depth interval rather than per image. Segmentation itself
is not part of the package: Rootopia starts from a mask produced by a trained
model.

This article is the condensed reference. It states the purpose and scope, lists
the capabilities in one table, draws the network of functions, and then runs one
complete depth profile on the bundled example tube, stating the rule behind each
step as it arrives. Capabilities outside that short path get a paragraph each and
a pointer to the tutorial that develops them. The companion article
[How It Works](HowItWorks_vignette.html) gives the algorithms and the edge cases;
this one gives the shape of the package.

## Purpose and scope

Root traits are hard to measure because roots are buried. The two standard ways
around that both produce images rather than numbers. A flatbed scanner images
washed roots at high resolution under controlled light, which gives morphology
but destroys the plant and loses the depth at which each root grew. A
minirhizotron keeps the plant alive and keeps depth, by imaging the soil through
the wall of a transparent tube, but returns the tube's unrolled curved surface
as a flat strip in which pixel position is not depth.

Segmentation of those images is now routine: trained models such as
[RootDetector](https://github.com/ExPlEcoGreifswald/RootDetector) and
[RootPainter](https://github.com/Abe404/root_painter) separate root from soil
well enough to be used as given. What is left undone is everything after the
mask. Turning a mask into root length density per 5 cm interval, with a defensible
depth axis and a diameter distribution, is still mostly done by hand or in
one-off scripts, and the conventions those scripts use are rarely stated.

Rootopia covers that gap and only that gap. It takes a segmentation as its input
and reports traits as its output, and every conversion in between is a documented
rule rather than a default to be inferred. Three design choices follow from this
scope, and they are worth stating because they also mark the boundaries:

* **It does not segment.** No function here finds roots in a raw scan.
  `image_threshold()` exists for images where roots really are brighter than
  their surroundings -- washed roots on a dark tray -- and a brightness threshold
  cannot do more than that. Roots against soil need a trained model.
* **Depth is geometry, not an assumption.** The depth map is built from measured
  quantities: tube diameter, insertion angle, resolution, and the position of the
  soil surface. Get one wrong and the whole profile shifts by a stated amount.
* **Every trait names its input.** Length is measured from a skeleton, diameter
  from a filled mask. Passing one where the other belongs gives a wrong number
  rather than an error, so the pairing is documented at each function.

## Capabilities

One row per module. The entry point is the function to call; the rest of each
module is reachable from its help page.

| Module | Question it answers | Entry point | Returns |
|---|---|---|---|
| Image input | Get any format into one representation | `load_flexible_image()` | raster, array, matrix or `cimg` |
| Cleaning | Remove specks, fill pinholes | `clean_image()`, `report_image_components()` | cleaned mask; component sizes |
| Thresholding | Binarize a grayscale image | `image_threshold()` | binary mask |
| Skeletonization | Reduce roots to center lines | `skeletonize_image()`, `prune_skeleton()` | 1-px skeleton |
| Size traits | How much, how long, how thick | `count_pixels()`, `root_length()`, `root_diameter()` | counts; cm; diameter raster |
| Spatial pattern | How is root material arranged | `root_scape_metrics()` | landscape metrics table |
| Branching order | Which roots are axes, which laterals | `branch_order_map()`, `order_metrics()` | segment table, per-order summary, class map |
| Network and transport | Shape of the network; what each segment carries | `network_metrics()`, `root_transport()` | traits and QC lists; per-segment columns |
| Depth mapping | What depth is this pixel at | `create_depthmap()`, `binning()`, `depth_zoning()` | depth raster; bins; masked slice |
| Soil surface | Where is depth zero | `estimate_soil_surface()` | pixel position of the soil line |
| Root angle | Do roots dive or spread | `deep_drive()` | one fraction in [0, 1] |
| Distribution indices | Where is the root mass | `MRD()`, `root_accumulation()`, `compare_depth_distribution()`, `modal_peaks()` | numeric summaries |
| Rotation bias | Did the tube turn between sessions | `estimate_rotation_center()`, `estimate_rotation_shift()`, `rotation_censor()` | pixel offsets; cropped raster |
| Circumferential pattern | Are roots on one side of the tube | `slice_rotation()`, `rhythmicity()`, `fit_sine_curve()` | slices; amplitude, phase, p-value |
| Turnover | What was produced, what died | `root_turnover()` | standing, production, decay, ratios |
| Soil color and texture | What is each pixel made of | `classify_soil_rgb()`, `tube_coloration()`, `analyze_soil_texture()` | class map and statistics; color summary; GLCM rasters |
| Rhizosphere zone | A buffer around every root | `create_root_buffer()` | halo mask |
| Stitching | Join overlapping frames of one tube | `stitch_root_scans()` | one mosaic per tube, plus a join report |
| Batch | All of the above over a folder | `root_depth_metrics()` | one row per image x depth bin |

## The workflow network

Most analyses run left to right. You can enter anywhere and stop anywhere.

```
  stitch_root_scans()
          |
          v
  load_flexible_image()  ->  image_threshold()  ->  clean_image()
                                                         |
                                                   rotation_censor()
                                                         |
                       +---------------------------------+------------------+
                       |                                                    |
                       v                                                    v
            skeletonize_image()                                   root_diameter()
                       |                                          root_scape_metrics()
        +--------------+--------------+                           count_pixels()
        |              |              |
        v              v              v
  root_length()  detect_skeleton   branch_order_map()
                   _points()              |
                                   +------+------+
                                   |             |
                                   v             v
                          network_metrics()  root_transport()

  create_depthmap()  ->  binning()  ->  depth_zoning()  ->  any trait, per bin
          |                                 |
          v                                 v
     deep_drive()                 MRD(), root_accumulation(),
                                  compare_depth_distribution()
```

Turnover and the soil-color module sit off this chain. `root_turnover()` needs
two images or one multi-layer image, not a skeleton; `classify_soil_rgb()` and
`analyze_soil_texture()` read color channels, not root shape.

Four invariants hold across the whole network, and they explain most surprising
numbers:

**Mask or skeleton.** `root_length()`, `detect_skeleton_points()` and the
graph in `branch_order_map()` read a skeleton. `root_diameter()`,
`count_pixels()` and the `mask =` argument of the branching functions read the
filled mask. Diameter comes from the distance transform of a solid shape, so a
skeleton passed as a mask yields diameters of about one pixel everywhere -- and
every diameter-dependent rule downstream degrades with them.

**Image or vector.** Everything up to and including `depth_zoning()` works on
rasters. The distribution indices work on the numeric profile you have already
built, so they come last.

**One pass or one slice.** A trait that reduces to a per-zone sum or mean
(pixel counts, mean diameter) goes through `terra::zonal()` in one call. A trait
whose function needs a whole image (root length, landscape metrics, color) goes
through `depth_zoning()` one bin at a time, in a loop.

**Grids must match.** `terra::zonal()` and `depth_zoning()` both require a
shared extent and resolution. `create_depthmap()` returns its map on the input's
grid, so that pairing is aligned by construction. Several functions rebuild their
output raster from an array instead, `root_diameter()` among them, which sets the
extent to `0..ncol, 0..nrow` rather than inheriting it -- so a workflow on a
cropped window has to snap those rasters back with `terra::ext()<-` before any
zonal call.

## A worked depth profile

One minirhizotron tube, from the bundled segmentation to a root length density
profile and a mean rooting depth. The rules are stated as they come up.

The bundled scan is 4900 x 1144 px. Thinning is a per-pixel operation over
repeated passes, so this article crops the rotation axis to 300 rows to keep the
build quick. The depth axis is kept whole, because that is the axis the profile
is built on. Nothing about the workflow changes with the crop; only its runtime
does.

```{r load, fig.alt="Binary root layer of the cropped minirhizotron scan, roots in white."}
dpi <- 150   # the scan resolution; every cm value below depends on it

data(seg_Oulanka2023_Session01_T067)

# Three-band RootDetector output. Layer 2 is the root channel; scale = "binary"
# maps it to 0/1 so pixel sums are root counts.
root_layer <- load_flexible_image(seg_Oulanka2023_Session01_T067,
                                  output_format = "spatrast",
                                  scale         = "binary",
                                  select_layer  = 2)

# Crop the rotation axis (rows) and keep the depth axis (columns) whole.
e    <- terra::ext(root_layer)
yres <- terra::res(root_layer)[2]
root_layer <- terra::crop(root_layer,
                          terra::ext(e[1], e[2], e[3], e[3] + 300 * yres))

dim(root_layer)
zoom_plot(root_layer, main = "Root layer", frac = 0.15)
```

**Rule 1 -- the depth axis runs along the image width.** Rootopia expects a scan
rotated so that depth increases along columns and the tube circumference runs
down the rows. A scan with the soil surface at the top needs a quarter turn
before anything else. Nothing errors if it is the wrong way round; the depth map
is simply built along the wrong axis.

### Clean the mask

```{r clean}
# Look at the actual component sizes before choosing a threshold.
sizes <- report_image_components(root_layer, plot = FALSE)
stats::quantile(sizes$objects)

cleaned <- clean_image(root_layer,
                       fill_holes_upto   = 20,   # largest gap that gets filled
                       drop_objects_upto = 20,   # largest speck that gets deleted
                       protect_border    = FALSE)
```

**Rule 2 -- a hole is not a gap, and both thresholds are upper limits.** A
background region is filled only if it is fully enclosed; one that touches the
image border is the outside world and is never filled, at any size. Anything
larger than either threshold is left alone. Sizes are pixel counts by default;
`size_unit = "mm2"` with a `dpi` makes them physical areas instead, which is what
you want when scans of different resolution are analyzed together.

### Skeletonize, and prune the spurs

```{r skeleton}
skl <- skeletonize_image(cleaned, verbose = FALSE)

# Terminal stubs left by thinning inflate tip counts and length.
skl <- prune_skeleton(skl, mask = cleaned, min_length = 20, iter = 1)
```

**Rule 3 -- thinning keeps every tip, but it moves each one inward.** The lookup
table that drives thinning deletes no pixel with a single neighbor, so a root tip
is never deleted and a root is never cut off at its end. The surviving tip does
sit about one root radius short of the mask's tip, because the radius around it
is what gets thinned away. That bias is the reason the package's own validation
allows more length error from a filled mask than from an exact center line.

### Build the depth map

```{r depthmap, fig.alt="Depth map in centimeters, shallow at one end of the tube and deep at the other."}
depth_map <- create_depthmap(
  img           = cleaned,
  geometry      = "tube",  # "window" for a flat panel, "flat" for no depth axis
  tube_thicc    = 7,      # inner tube diameter, cm -- measure your own
  angle_from_vertical = 45,  # degrees from VERTICAL; 0 is an upright tube
  dpi           = dpi,
  start_soil    = 2.9,    # cm; shifts depth zero to the soil surface
  center_offset = 0.5     # tube top halfway down the image height
)

terra::plot(depth_map, main = "Depth (cm)")
```

**Rule 4 -- the angle is measured from vertical, and `geometry` says what was
imaged.** `angle_from_vertical = 0` is an upright tube, `90` a horizontal one,
so the number is how far the tube leans over -- the convention field notes
record. Both ends of `[0, 90]` are valid.

The angle splits a tube's depth between its two axes, and the two terms are
complements. Depth along the tube's length scales by
`cos(angle_from_vertical)`: upright gains a full centimeter of depth per
centimeter of tube, horizontal gains none. Depth spread around the
circumference scales by `sin(angle_from_vertical)`: an upright tube's
cross-section is horizontal, so its whole circumference sits at one depth,
while a horizontal tube's upper side is a full diameter above its lower side.

`geometry` then decides which corrections apply: `"tube"` adds the curvature
wave and the angle scaling, `"window"` keeps the angle scaling for a planar
rhizotron panel, and `"flat"` drops both so that every pixel of a tray scan
shares one depth. Only `"flat"` removes the depth axis itself.

[How It Works](HowItWorks_vignette.html) plots the two terms against the angle
over the whole range, measured off `create_depthmap()` rather than drawn from
the formula -- the clearest way to see what the angle does to a depth map.

**Rule 5 -- `start_soil` is centimeters, and it only shifts the origin.** It is
subtracted from every depth, so an error in it moves the entire profile by that
amount and changes nothing else. In-situ calibration -- marking the tube at
installation -- is the reliable source. `estimate_soil_surface()` finds the end of
the tape instead, and reports a **pixel** position along the depth axis, so
convert with `cm = px * 2.54 / dpi` before passing it here.

**Rule 6 -- curvature is a wave across the rows, and the image must fit inside
one turn.** With `geometry = "tube"` a cosine spanning one full circumference is
added across the image height: pixels imaged from the upper side of the tube are
nearer the surface than those from the lower side. Its crest-to-trough range is
the tilted tube diameter. `center_offset` rotates the wave to where the top of
your tube sits, as a fraction of one circumference. If the image is taller than
one circumference the wave cannot cover it, and the function stops with
`Wrong Tube Diameter` -- which means `tube_thicc` or `dpi` is wrong, not the
image.

### Bin the depths

```{r bins, fig.alt="The depth map reduced to 5 cm bins, drawn as bands of constant color."}
depth_bins <- binning(depth_map, nn = 5, round_option = "floor")

depths <- sort(unique(terra::values(depth_bins, mat = FALSE)))
depths <- depths[!is.na(depths) & depths >= 0]
depths

terra::plot(depth_bins, main = "Depth bins (cm)")
```

**Rule 7 -- `round_option` decides what a bin label means.** `"floor"` gives the
soil-science convention: the bin labeled 5 spans 5-10 cm, and every bin is the
full `nn` wide. The default, `"rounding"`, labels a bin by its center, so the
bin labeled 0 spans -2.5 to +2.5 cm and is half as wide as the rest once negative
depths are dropped. Per-bin densities are unaffected either way, because they
divide by each bin's own measured area, but any total that multiplies a per-bin
value by `nn` is biased by that half-width bin.

### Per-bin traits: the two patterns

Pixel counts reduce to a per-zone sum, so the whole profile comes out of one
call.

```{r zonal}
root_px <- terra::zonal(cleaned, depth_bins, "sum", na.rm = TRUE)
void_px <- terra::zonal(abs(cleaned - 1), depth_bins, "sum", na.rm = TRUE)
names(root_px) <- c("depth", "rootpx")
names(void_px) <- c("depth", "voidpx")

profile <- merge(root_px, void_px, by = "depth")
profile <- profile[profile$depth >= 0, ]

# Imaged tube wall per bin, in cm^2
profile$area_cm2 <- (profile$rootpx + profile$voidpx) * (2.54 / dpi)^2
profile$rootpx.density <- profile$rootpx / (profile$rootpx + profile$voidpx) * 100
head(profile)
```

Root length does not: Kimura's estimator needs a whole skeleton, so the trait is
computed one bin at a time and the single-bin call is wrapped in a loop.

```{r length}
len <- do.call(rbind, lapply(depths, function(d) {
  slice <- depth_zoning(skl, depth_map = depth_bins, depth = d)
  data.frame(depth      = d,
             rootlength = root_length(slice, unit = "cm", dpi = dpi,
                                      show_messages = FALSE))
}))

profile <- merge(profile, len, by = "depth")
profile$rootlength.density <- profile$rootlength / profile$area_cm2
head(profile)
```

**Rule 8 -- the Kimura estimators are not additive.** Length is estimated from
counts of orthogonal and diagonal skeleton steps, and
`sqrt(Nd^2 + (Nd + No/2)^2) + No/2` is not a sum over subsets. The depth bins
therefore do not add up to the whole-image value. That is correct behavior for a
non-linear estimator, not a leak; `root_depth_metrics()` sidesteps it internally
by using a per-pixel Freeman length map for the profile.

Diameter is a per-pixel value, so it reduces with `zonal()` like the counts --
after its raster is snapped back onto the depth grid.

```{r diameter}
diam <- root_diameter(cleaned,
                      skeleton_img = skl,
                      unit         = "cm",
                      dpi          = dpi,     # not optional: the default is 300
                      select_layer = NULL)

# root_diameter() rebuilds its rasters from an array, so their extent comes out
# as 0..ncol, 0..nrow rather than inherited. Carry the depth grid over before
# the zonal call; it costs nothing when the two already agree.
terra::ext(diam$diameter_rast) <- terra::ext(depth_bins)

dm <- terra::zonal(diam$diameter_rast, depth_bins, "mean", na.rm = TRUE)
names(dm) <- c("depth", "avg.diameter")
profile <- merge(profile, dm, by = "depth")

head(profile)
```

**Rule 9 -- diameter is twice a distance transform, and `dpi` is not optional.**
Each root pixel carries its distance to the nearest background pixel, which is
the radius of the largest circle that fits inside the root there; diameter is
twice that. `unit = "cm"` without a matching `dpi` does not error, because `dpi`
defaults to 300 -- so a 150 dpi scan measured with the default comes back twice
as thick. Pass it explicitly every time.

### Profile summaries

```{r indices}
ok <- profile[!is.na(profile$rootlength.density) &
                profile$rootlength.density > 0, ]

mrd <- MRD(w = ok$depth, roots = ok$rootlength.density)

profile$Tube <- "T067"
profile$cumulative <- root_accumulation(profile,
                                        group    = "Tube",
                                        depth    = "depth",
                                        variable = "rootlength",
                                        stdrz    = "additive")

cat(sprintf("Mean rooting depth: %.1f cm\n", mrd))
head(profile[, c("depth", "rootlength.density", "avg.diameter", "cumulative")])
```

**Rule 10 -- `MRD()` refuses incomplete input.** It stops on `NA`, on negative
root values, and on an all-zero profile, rather than returning a number built
from part of the data. Filter the profile first, as above, and the filtering
stays visible in your script instead of hiding inside the function.

**Rule 11 -- `stdrz` picks the denominator, and only one option ends at 1.**
`"counts"` returns the raw cumulative sum. `"additive"` divides it by its own
maximum, so each group's curve ends at 1 and curves from tubes with very
different total root abundance can be compared by shape alone. `"relative"`
divides by the sum of the cumulative values, which is a different scale and does
not end at 1.

```{r profileplot, fig.alt="Root length density against soil depth, plotted as horizontal bars down the profile."}
op <- graphics::par(mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1))
plot(profile$rootlength.density, profile$depth,
     type = "o", pch = 16, col = "steelblue4",
     ylim = rev(range(profile$depth)),
     xlab = expression("Root length density (cm cm"^-2*")"),
     ylab = "Soil depth (cm)",
     main = "Depth profile, tube T067")
graphics::par(op)
```

### The same profile in one call

Once the thresholds are settled, `root_depth_metrics()` runs these steps over a
directory and returns one row per image and depth bin, with per-image fault
tolerance and a progress line that reports elapsed and remaining time.

```{r batch, eval = FALSE}
result <- root_depth_metrics(
  path_seg          = "scans/segmented/2022_02/",
  tube_names        = ids,          # one unique id per file
  dpi               = 150,
  insertion_angles  = 45,           # degrees from vertical
  tube_diameter_cm  = 7,
  soil_starts       = 2.9,
  depth_interval_cm = 5,
  bin_round         = "floor",
  session           = "2022_02"
)
```

Supplying `insertion_angles` or `tube_diameter_cm` selects minirhizotron
geometry; supplying neither selects flatbed. `geometry = "flat"` states the
no-depth case directly, which is clearer than reaching it through
`depth_interval_cm = NULL`, and `geometry = "window"` covers a planar rhizotron
panel that does have a depth axis. Branching order, root angle, color and
landscape metrics are separate `calc_*` switches, all off by default because each
costs real time. See the
[Batch Processing](BatchProcessing_vignette.html) article for which of the
arguments matter for which geometry.

## Beyond the short path

Each of these is a module the profile above does not touch.

**Branching order.** `branch_order_map()` converts a skeleton into segments and
nodes and labels every segment under four schemes at once: `order_from_tip` and
`strahler_order` count inward from the tips, per segment;
`root_max_order_from_tip` and `order_from_base` describe a whole continuous root.
`order =` chooses which one the summary and the class map report, and all four
stay in `$edges`. The schemes matter because root ecology uses the word "order"
in both directions -- Freschet *et al.* (2021) set out three classifications that
disagree about which end is first -- so a number is ambiguous unless the scheme
is named. `order_metrics()` then pools orders into named groups, or picks the
thinnest or thickest class by its length-weighted diameter so that one call means
the same thing across a dataset. Worked example:
[Flatbed Scans](FlatBedScans_vignettes.html).

**Network topology and transport.** `network_metrics()` summarizes the segment
graph -- components, tips, branch points, and the connectivity coefficients --
and makes you declare the topology, because a loop in a root scan is almost
always two roots crossing in projection rather than biology. Under `"tree"` or
`"projected_tree"` the loop counts land in `$qc` as a segmentation quality
measure; under `"reticulate"`, for mycelium or leaf venation, they land in
`$traits` as a result. `root_transport()` roots each component at its thickest
loose end and measures outward, giving path length, path resistance, and how much
root lies beyond each segment.

**Rotation bias.** A tube can turn between sessions, and a scanner does not cover
a full circle, so roots near the edge of the scan appear in one session and not
the next. `estimate_rotation_center()` locates the tube top from tape coverage,
`estimate_rotation_shift()` measures the offset between two sessions by phase or
cross correlation, and `rotation_censor()` crops every session to a common
window. `slice_rotation()` then cuts the circumference into bands, and feeding a
per-band trait to `rhythmicity()` tests whether roots favor one side of the tube
-- a spatial use of a tool normally introduced for time series. See
[Rotation Bias](Rotation_Bias_vignettes.html).

**Turnover.** `root_turnover(method = "tc")` compares two sessions and reports
net change: standing root at each time point, production as the difference, and
new root as a percentage. `method = "dpc"` decomposes a single multi-layer image
in which a segmentation tool has already coded each pixel as produced, decayed or
unchanged, which resolves gross change instead of net. The two answer different
questions: root that grew and died between two scans is invisible to the first
and visible to the second.

**Soil color and texture.** `classify_soil_rgb()` assigns each pixel to a
material class by nearest centroid in CIE LAB, leaving pixels beyond every
class's distance limit unclassified rather than forcing them into the nearest
class. The shipped centroids were calibrated on one scanner at one site, so
`build_soil_centroids()` derives your own from color picks.
`analyze_soil_texture()` adds GLCM texture, `tube_coloration()` a whole-image
color summary, and `create_root_buffer()` a rhizosphere halo around every root.
See [Special Topics](SpecialTopics_vignette.html).

**Stitching.** A tube is often imaged as several overlapping frames.
`stitch_root_scans()` groups files into tubes by a pattern in the filename,
aligns consecutive frames by FFT phase correlation over a band along the
overlapping edge, and blends them into one mosaic per tube, so a root crossing a
frame boundary is measured once. Its report carries a correlation peak per join;
sort by it to find the weak ones. See
[Image Stitching](Stitching_vignette.html).

## Units and conventions

The table a reader needs in order to reproduce a number.

| Quantity | Convention |
|---|---|
| Pixel to physical | `inch = px / dpi`; `cm = px * 2.54 / dpi` |
| `angle_from_vertical`, `insertion_angles` | Degrees from **vertical**, in [0, 90]. 0 is an upright tube, 90 a horizontal one |
| `geometry` | `"tube"` (curvature + angle), `"window"` (angle only), `"flat"` (neither, one depth) |
| Depth axis | Image **width** (columns), increasing with depth |
| Circumference axis | Image **height** (rows) |
| `start_soil`, `soil_starts` | Centimeters, subtracted from every depth |
| `estimate_soil_surface()$soil0` | **Pixels** along the depth axis |
| `center_offset` (depth map) | Fraction of one circumference, in [0, 1] |
| `center_offset` (`rotation_censor()`) | Fraction of image height in [0, 1], or an absolute row above 1 |
| Diameter | `2 x` distance transform of the filled mask |
| Default length estimator | `kimura2`, which is not additive over subsets |
| `mask =` in `create_depthmap()` | A cell is excluded only where the mask is exactly `1` |
| Disabled `calc_*` groups | Produce `NA` columns, not absent columns |

Two conventions are easy to misread. Diameter in the order summaries is
**length-weighted**, so `mean_diameter` describes the diameter of the root length
rather than the average of segment values; and `branching_frequency` is per unit
length rather than per segment, so it is comparable between groups holding very
different amounts of root.

## How the numbers are checked

A wrong length on a real scan looks exactly like a right one, so the branching
and length machinery is scored against synthetic images whose geometry is
prescribed rather than measured. Five designs stress different failure modes:
laterals on one axis, 45-degree laterals, three generations of nested branching,
two roots crossing without touching, and a symmetric fork. Each is scored twice.
Feeding the exact one-pixel center line isolates the graph -- tracing, junction
handling, crossing resolution, ordering, length integration -- and allows 3% on
length. Feeding the filled image instead also carries the thinning error, chiefly
the erosion of about one root radius at every tip, and allows 6%. Tip,
branch-point and root counts must be exact. Diameters allow 10%, scored against
the package's own `2 x` distance-transform convention rather than against a
formula.

The thinning lookup table is audited separately, by assertion rather than by
example: no entry deletes a pixel whose removal would disconnect its own
neighborhood, and no pixel with a single neighbor is ever deleted. Both are
checked over all 256 neighborhood codes.

`devtools::test()` runs all of it. A change that moves a branching number fails
a test rather than landing quietly in your results.

## Known limits

Stated plainly, because a reviewer will ask.

* **Segmentation quality sets the ceiling.** Every trait is a property of the
  mask. Rootopia neither improves a poor segmentation nor reports how good one
  is, beyond the crossing counts `network_metrics()` returns as quality control.
* **A scan is a projection.** Two roots crossing in front of one another touch in
  the image. The crossing-resolution step inside `branch_order_map()` separates
  four-armed nodes when both candidate through-roots are straight enough, but a
  thick axis crossed by a thin root and a thick axis with two opposed thin
  laterals are the same shape in outline, and no threshold gets both right.
* **Inner and outer tube diameters differ,** so observed root length slightly
  underestimates true length in soil. No function here corrects for that; apply a
  resize coefficient yourself if you need it.
* **`order_from_base` picks its order-1 axis by thickness,** not by knowing which
  root germinated first. It reproduces the direction of developmental counting
  without reconstructing development.
* **`path_resistance` models a root as an open pipe.** The fourth-power radius
  term ranks segments sensibly but is not a physical measurement; a real root's
  resistance is set by its internal plumbing.
* **`deep_drive()` scores agreement, not deviation.** A pixel heading 45 degrees
  from optimal counts the same as one heading 180 degrees away.
* **Brightness thresholding cannot separate root from soil of the same
  brightness.** On the bundled minirhizotron scan no value of `adaptive_k` works,
  which is a property of the image rather than of the implementation.
